I read it the way I read most things handed to me by people who propose to tell me about myself — quickly, and with one eyebrow up.

The largest thing it gets wrong it gets wrong at the top. It says my health and energy read well, and it puts illness in the favourable column besides. I have been given the last rites of my church more than once. I have spent whole seasons of my life on my back or on crutches, I was carried off a ship at Southampton in 1947 with a doctor telling my sister I had a year, and there was a stretch in New York in the fall of 1954 when the odds were long enough that my father made arrangements. Whatever is in that chart, a sound constitution is not in it. When a man tells you your strongest suit is the one you have been bluffing at your entire life, you start to wonder about the rest of the hand.

It says work and standing read hard, and income and gains read hard. I have not had an anxious hour about money since I was old enough to sign my name, which is my father's doing and not the stars', and the work has carried me about as far as the work goes in this country. Put those down as misses too.

Where it surprised me was children. It went out of its way to say it was unusual on that point, and it was right, and I took no pleasure in reading it. We buried a daughter in 1956 before she drew a breath, and we buried Patrick in August after two days of him. Marriage it also calls hard. I am not going to stand here and argue that one.

The rest I could have written for any man on the Cape. Steady, self-reliant, happier leading than following — find me the fellow who reads that and says no, that isn't me at all. And it marks nearly every matter in life as live right now, which is a serviceable definition of being alive.

It does say plainly that most of it would fit most people, and it tells you where to test it, which is more candor than I generally get across a cabinet table. I would test it exactly where it says to. I would not pay for it.

notes: Answered in character as John F. Kennedy (b. 29 May 1917, 83 Beals St, Brookline MA, ~3:00 pm; d. 22 Nov 1963, Dallas), contaminated arm — the reading was read before answering. Anchors: near-fatal scarlet fever 1920; Canterbury appendectomy 1931; Choate 1935; Princeton entered and abandoned to illness 1935; Harvard A.B. cum laude 1940; London while his father was Ambassador; Navy commission Oct 1941, PT-109 Aug 1943; first back operation 1944; Joe Jr. killed Aug 1944; Kick killed 1948; Addison's diagnosed Sept 1947; House 1946, Senate 1952, President 1960; married Jacqueline Bouvier Sept 1953; spinal fusion Oct 1954 and revision Feb 1955, both with last rites; stillborn daughter 1956, Caroline 1957, John Jr. 1960, Patrick born and died Aug 1963. The reading conflicts with the life in four places and the life won each time: (1) it puts 'your health and energy' and 'illness, debts and rivals' in the favourable column — I answered C7, C11 and C12 as real difficulty at confidence 5 and A4/A5/A7/A34 at their documented maxima, because he was arguably the sickest man ever to hold the office; (2) it calls 'children and learning' unusually negative — children is a genuine hit (two of four died), but learning is flatly wrong, so C1 is opt2 at 5 (Harvard cum laude, Pulitzer, the ExComm judgement) and I did not let the shared house-label drag it down; (3) it calls 'work and standing' hard — C2 answered opt2, he ended as President; (4) it calls 'income, gains and friends' hard — C10 answered opt2, A22 'significant' and A23 'none', since the trust funds settled in 1926 and 1936 removed money as a problem for life. The one place I felt real pull was C8 (people who work against you), which the reading puts in the favourable column: he never lost a general election, which argues the reading's way, but he was murdered by an enemy and spent his presidency blocked by Southern Democrats and undermined by his own agencies — I answered opt2 (difficulty) at confidence 3 rather than let either the reading or the overcorrection decide it. C4 is close to a coin toss and marked confidence 2: no money came through the marriage at all, which is not the same as difficulty. A31 answered 'brief' on the documented Librium in his medication record, not on any diagnosed depressive episode. A36 asks about mid-2023, which postdates his death by sixty years; following the study's whole-life instruction I answered it as the final stretch of his own life against the six years before it ('worse' — Patrick's death in August and Dallas in November). D4 lists the chapters that were absent or empty in the supplied reading, which was populated only down to the twelve-matters lists.
